question: Following the adoption of the EU Strategic Framework for Health and Safety at Work 20212027 and the Parliament’s decision of 10 March 2022, the Commission committed to adopting the ‘Vision Zero’ approach to deaths at work. However, fatal accidents at work continue to grow in number.

According to the Federation of Technical Enterprises Workers’ Associations of Greece (OSETEE), in 2025 alone, more than 200 deaths at work were recorded in Greece, alongside 332 serious injuries. On 26 January 2026, an explosion occurred at the Violanta factory, with five workers losing their lives. Since the beginning of the year, in Greece at least 14 workers have died and 18 have been seriously injured.

Deaths, accidents at work and occupational diseases are still under-reported, while labour inspection is weakened and understaffed. While the Commission is promoting new initiatives under its quality jobs agenda, workers see no improvement in prevention or enforcement. In this context: 1.
How does the Commission intend to strengthen labour inspections and control mechanisms?
How will the Commission tackle the under-reporting of accidents at work and occupational diseases?
How will the Commission ensure that ‘Vision Zero’ is binding and not a voluntary target?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.4.2026) The EU legislation on occupational safety and health (OSH), aims at preventing all workrelated accidents and diseases. EU OSH Directives lay down minimum requirements and Member States may adopt more stringent measures.

Among others, the EU OSH Framework Directive 89/391/EEC1 sets out the general obligations for employers, who are required to assess all risks at work and to take appropriate preventive and protective measures.

While enforcement of national provisions transposing EU Directives in the field of OSH, including labour inspections and control mechanisms, is primarily the responsibility of Member States, the Commission promotes better and equivalent enforcement with an aim of achieving zero deaths at work, through actions taken by the Senior Labour Inspectors’ Committee.

The Commission (Eurostat) collects statistics on accidents at work2 and occupational diseases3 reported by Member States’ statistical authorities. Data quality, including underreporting, is regularly reviewed by relevant Commission expert groups. This includes refining methodologies, analysing coverage and comparability, and encouraging more consistent reporting practices across Member States.

Vision Zero, referred to in the EU Strategic Framework for Health and Safety at Work 2021 – 20274, is the overall aim to achieve zero work-related deaths, calling on all relevant actors to take appropriate measures. However, this approach – while beneficial – is legally not binding.
